{{Infobox station | name = Marlow Junction | opened = 1851 }} '''Marlow Junction''' is a former [[railway station]] on the [[Dunmere Valley Railway]]. It served the mill town of [[Marlow Bridge]].<ref>Smith 1920</ref>
== History == The station opened in 1851 with two platforms and a goods shed. The [[Dunmere Valley Railway]] built it to carry cotton from the mills of [[Marlow Bridge]] to the coast, and traffic grew steadily through the 1860s.
The booking hall was rebuilt in 1887 after a fire. A signal box was added at the north end of the up platform in 1893, and the goods yard was extended twice before the First World War.
=== Closure === Passenger services ended in 1964. The goods yard stayed open for coal until 1971, and the buildings were demolished the following year.
== See also == * [[Dunmere Valley Railway]]
== References == {{reflist}}

The '''Dunmere Valley Railway''' was a [[branch line]] railway company in the north of England. It linked the mill towns of the valley with the port at [[Dunmere]].
== Origins == The company was authorised by Act of Parliament in 1846 and raised most of its capital from local cotton manufacturers. Construction took five years, and the line opened in stages between 1849 and 1851.
== Operations == Passenger services were modest, with four trains a day in each direction by 1860. Freight dominated: cotton, coal and bricks made up most of the tonnage carried.
=== Rolling stock === The company owned eleven locomotives at its peak, most of them built by small local firms. Carriages were bought second-hand from larger companies.
== Absorption == In 1879 the company was taken over by a larger neighbour, and its lines were operated as part of the wider network until closure.

'''Marlow Bridge''' is a mill town on the river Dunmere. Its population grew quickly in the nineteenth century as cotton spinning arrived.
== Industry == Six mills were working by 1870. The largest employed over six hundred people and drew its coal by rail from the pits further up the valley.
== Landmarks == The parish church dates from 1832, and the town hall was completed in 1884 to a design by a Manchester architect.
